This chapter fits the He et al. [-@he2010] seasonal SEIR measles
model to synthetic data generated from the published MLE. Synthetic
recovery localizes failure: we know the answer, the data come from
the same process the inference assumes, so any failure points to
either a modelling artifact or an inference artifact, not to model
misspecification.

The chapter shows two fit attempts on the same synthetic dataset.
**Round 1** uses camdl's package defaults — a deliberately minimal
budget that exposes what defaults do on a hard problem. **Round 2**
scales up to budgets comparable to standard pomp-vignette settings
[@king2016pomp]. Throughout, **each chain keeps the same color
across all diagnostic plots** so an outlier on the log-likelihood
trace can be identified as the same outlier on the pair plot. A
detailed historical version of this analysis with extensive
diagnostic callouts is preserved at
[`he2010-synthetic-v1`](he2010-synthetic-v1.qmd).

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false
import os, sys, subprocess, tomllib, io
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Import shared book-level helpers from <book root>/_lib/
_BOOK_ROOT = Path("/Users/vsb/projects/work/camdl-book")
sys.path.insert(0, str(_BOOK_ROOT))
from _lib.pair_plot import pair_plot_chains, load_chain_traces, chain_color_palette
from _lib.cli import run_cli
from _lib.profile_plot import plot_profile_panels

GREY = "#666666"
plt.rcParams.update({
    "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.labelcolor": GREY, "xtick.color": GREY, "ytick.color": GREY,
    "axes.edgecolor": GREY, "legend.edgecolor": GREY,
})

VDIR = Path("he2010")
MODEL  = VDIR / "models/he2010_london.camdl"
PARAMS = VDIR / "params/he2010_london.toml"
SYNTH  = VDIR / "data/he2010_synthetic_obs.tsv"
REAL   = VDIR / "data/he2010_london_cases.tsv"

# Truth values from params/he2010_london.toml
TRUTH = {"R0": 56.8, "alpha": 0.976, "amplitude": 0.554,
         "gamma": 0.0832, "s0": 0.0297, "sigma": 0.0791}
TRUTH_LL = -5982.7   # 16k×8 reference clean PF eval at truth
PARAMS_LIST = ["R0", "alpha", "gamma", "amplitude", "sigma", "s0"]
BOUNDS = {"R0": (5.0, 100.0), "alpha": (0.5, 1.0),
          "gamma": (0.02, 0.2), "amplitude": (0.1, 0.9),
          "sigma": (0.02, 0.2), "s0": (0.001, 0.5)}

def assert_fresh(path, *deps, hint=""):
    if not path.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"{path} missing — {hint}")
    pm = path.stat().st_mtime
    for d in deps:
        if Path(d).stat().st_mtime > pm:
            raise RuntimeError(f"{path} older than {d}. Run: {hint}")
    return path

assert_fresh(SYNTH, MODEL, PARAMS, hint="cd vignettes/he2010 && make sim")

def _find_fit(prefix):
    hits = sorted((VDIR / "results/fits").glob(f"{prefix}/real/fit_42"))
    return next((h for h in reversed(hits)
                 if (h / "scout/fit_state.toml").exists()), None)

R1_ROOT = _find_fit("fit-*")
if R1_ROOT is None:
    raise RuntimeError("no R1 fit. Run: cd vignettes/he2010 && make fit-r1")
R1_SCOUT = R1_ROOT / "scout"
```

## 1. Forward-simulation validation

Before any inference work, we validate that camdl's chain-binomial
backend produces the same forward-simulation distribution at the He
et al. MLE as the pomp reference [@king2016pomp]. Recovery
experiments against a buggy simulator are meaningless.

```{python}
#| label: envelope-smoke
#| echo: false
run_cli("python validation/envelope_smoke.py", cwd="he2010",
        echo="python validation/envelope_smoke.py")
```

## 2. The synthetic dataset

One synthetic dataset, seed 42, 21 years of weekly notifications,
generated from the He et al. MLE.

The synthetic dataset is produced by `make sim`, which runs:

```{.bash}
camdl simulate models/he2010_london.camdl \
    --params params/he2010_london.toml \
    --backend chain_binomial --dt 1 --seed 42 \
    --obs-only data/he2010_synthetic_obs.tsv
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-synth-vs-real
#| fig-cap: "Synthetic dataset (top) generated at the He et al. MLE under seed 42 vs. real London notifications 1944–1964 (bottom). Visual similarity is not the validation criterion — see callout."
synth = pl.read_csv(SYNTH, separator="\t")
real  = pl.read_csv(REAL,  separator="\t")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 4.5), sharex=True)
axes[0].plot(synth["time"], synth["weekly_cases"], color="#3366cc", linewidth=0.8)
axes[0].set_ylabel("synth weekly cases")
axes[1].plot(real["time"], real["cases"], color="#222222", linewidth=0.8)
axes[1].set_ylabel("real weekly cases")
axes[1].set_xlabel("time (days from 1944-01-07)")
fig.tight_layout()
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Subtle and pernicious: cherry-picking synthetic seeds

A natural temptation is to *select* a synthetic draw that "looks
like" the real data. **Do not.** Once you filter draws by features
of the real data, the inference is no longer a clean recovery
test — you have leaked structure of the real data into the
ground truth. The pipeline either recovers, or it doesn't; the
data realization is what it is. Same applies to *any* tuning
informed by the truth dataset (bounds, cooling, particles).
:::

## 3. Round 1: defaults

camdl's package defaults: 8 chains × 500 particles × 30 iterations,
cooling = 0.70.

The fit configuration:

```{python}
#| label: show-r1-config
#| echo: false
run_cli("cat fit.toml", cwd="he2010",
        echo="cat fit.toml", max_lines=80)
```

The fit is launched by `make fit-r1`, which runs:

```{.bash}
camdl fit run fit.toml --seed 42 --progress plain
```

```{python}
#| label: r1-load
#| echo: false
t1 = load_chain_traces(R1_SCOUT)
chain_ids_r1 = sorted(t1["chain"].unique().to_list())
COLORS_R1 = chain_color_palette(chain_ids_r1)
state1 = tomllib.loads((R1_SCOUT / "fit_state.toml").read_text())
```

### Per-chain log-likelihood trajectories

```{python}
#| label: fig-r1-ll-trajectories
#| fig-cap: "R1 per-chain log-likelihood across IF2 iterations. Each iter's value is the IF2 cloud log-likelihood at 500 particles (`if2_perturbed_loglik`, dense per-iter trace). Chain colors are consistent across every R1 figure in this section. Truth at ℓ ≈ −5983 (dashed). Chains in the bad-s₀ basin dive to ll ≈ −9000 around iter 13 before partially recovering as cooling concentrates them."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
for c in chain_ids_r1:
    sub = t1.filter(pl.col("chain") == c).sort("iteration")
    ax.plot(sub["iteration"], sub["if2_perturbed_loglik"],
            color=COLORS_R1[c], linewidth=1.4, alpha=0.85,
            label=f"chain {c}")
ax.axhline(TRUTH_LL, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
ax.set_xlabel("IF2 iteration")
ax.set_ylabel("if2_perturbed_loglik (cloud ll, 500p)")
ax.set_title("R1: per-chain log-likelihood across iterations")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="center left",
          bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5))
fig.tight_layout()
```

### R1 fit summary

```{python}
#| label: r1-summary
#| echo: false
run_cli(f"camdl fit summary {R1_ROOT} --no-color",
        echo=f"camdl fit summary {R1_ROOT}")
```

R1 fails both legs of the compound gate, but **marginally**: Â on R₀
and α is in the 1.05–1.06 band — chains agree on the same ridge
basin within sampling noise, just slightly above the gate's strict
1.01 threshold. The pair plot shows what's happening: γ, σ,
amplitude all cluster tightly across chains; R₀, α, s₀ spread along
the analytic identifiability ridge ($\beta(t)\,(I+\iota)^\alpha$
flat to first order in the (s₀, α) direction).

The winner sits at R₀ ≈ 67, α ≈ 0.72, s₀ ≈ 0.16 — an "alternative
MLE" along the ridge, not He et al.'s published values (R₀ = 56.8,
α = 0.976, s₀ = 0.030). ll = −6173.6 vs truth at −5982.7, a 191-nat
gap. Important context: when camdl-vignettes fit the *real* London
data, it converged to a similar ridge point (R₀ ≈ 43, α ≈ 0.77,
s₀ ≈ 0.06) — different basin point, same ridge structure. **The
ridge is real, not an artifact**; He et al. drove their published
MLE through bound-narrowing rounds and informed start values.

## 4. Refine

Scout's gate failed marginally (Â at 1.05 vs threshold 1.01) but the
chains agree on the ridge basin. Refine starts from scout's
loglik-eval winner and runs a small, cold IF2 ensemble (camdl
defaults: 4 chains × 1000 particles × 50 iterations × cf50 = 0.05)
to drive the parameters toward the local MLE within that basin.
Launched by `camdl fit run fit.toml --seed 42 --allow-nonconverged-scout`.

```{python}
#| label: refine-summary
#| echo: false
R1_REFINE_DIR = R1_ROOT / "refine"
if R1_REFINE_DIR.exists():
    run_cli(f"camdl fit summary {R1_ROOT} --stage refine --no-color",
            echo=f"camdl fit summary {R1_ROOT} --stage refine")
else:
    print("Refine not yet run. Run: camdl fit run fit.toml --seed 42 --allow-nonconverged-scout")
```

**Refine improved ll by 112 nats** (scout: −6173.6 → refine: −6061.2),
narrowing the gap to truth from 191 to 78 nats. The refine winner
sits at a different point on the same ridge — R₀ swung from
scout's 67 to refine's 32 (truth: 56.8) — illustrating ridge
flatness in (R₀, α). The 4 chains span only 94 nats in ll
(σ_max = 1.22 nats), tightly clustered.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Why refine's Â looks broken

The reported Â values for refine are extreme (Â on s₀ = 36.9, on
R₀ = 24.9). **These are statistical artifacts of cold cooling, not
real chain disagreement.** Â is camdl's chain-agreement statistic
for MLE-pipeline output (scout, refine, validate); it uses the same
$\sqrt{\hat V / W}$ formula as Gelman–Rubin's $\hat R$ for MCMC, but
applies it to IF2 parameter-mean trajectories rather than to
posterior samples. The renaming is deliberate: $\hat R$ in the MCMC
context implies "samples have mixed to a stationary distribution";
Â here only implies "independent stochastic optimizers ended up at
the same point in parameter space" — the math is the same, the
interpretation isn't.

The pathology specific to refine: with cf50 = 0.05, within-chain
parameter variance $W$ shrinks to near-zero by iter 25 (cooling
drives perturbation $\sigma_t / \sigma_0 \to 0$). When $W \to 0$,
$\hat A = \sqrt{\hat V / W}$ blows up regardless of how tight the
between-chain spread $\hat V$ is. The 4 refine chains here span
only 94 nats in loglik-eval ll and have winner θ̂ values within a
few percent of each other — the cold-cooled chains agree, the
statistic just can't see it.

The cross-stage signal `vs scout: Δ = +112 nats ✓` is the right
diagnostic for refine convergence, not Â. Camdl's gate machinery
currently applies the same Â test to refine as to scout, which
over-flags successful refines. Worth filing upstream.
:::

## 5. Profile likelihoods on s₀ and R₀

The pair plot suggested an identifiability ridge in (s₀, R₀, α).
Profile likelihoods are the formal diagnostic: at each grid value
of the profile parameter, *re-optimize* the other parameters via
IF2, evaluate the resulting MLE's log-likelihood. A flat profile
means the data does not identify that parameter; a peaked profile
(narrow at high resolution) means it does.

These are **true profile likelihoods**, not slice / conditional
likelihoods — at every grid point, the other parameters are
re-fit. Profiles started from the refine MLE (not truth — see
data-leakage rule).

```{python}
#| label: r3-profiles-load
#| echo: false
PROFS = Path("he2010/validation")
PROF_S0 = PROFS / "profile_s0.tsv"
PROF_R0 = PROFS / "profile_r0.tsv"
have_s0 = PROF_S0.exists()
have_r0 = PROF_R0.exists()
if not (have_s0 and have_r0):
    print("Profiles not yet present.")
    print(f"  s0 profile: {'✓' if have_s0 else '⏳ pending'}")
    print(f"  R0 profile: {'✓' if have_r0 else '⏳ pending'}")
    print("Run: cd vignettes/he2010 && make profiles")

def _load_profile(path):
    """Load a profile TSV, aliasing pre-`b8878e2` `best_loglik` to
    `loglik` so vignettes/he2010/validation/*.tsv generated against
    the older single-seed schema still resolve. Drop once the
    validation TSVs are regenerated against current camdl."""
    df = pl.read_csv(path, separator="\t", comment_prefix="#")
    if "best_loglik" in df.columns and "loglik" not in df.columns:
        df = df.rename({"best_loglik": "loglik"})
    return df
```

```{python}

S0_PANELS = ["loglik", "R0", "alpha", "gamma"]
```

## 6. Identifiability ridge — theory vs empirics

The profile-likelihood flatness is not random; it has a closed-form
analytical explanation rooted in the model's force-of-infection
expression. He et al. parameterise it as

$$\lambda(t) = \beta(t) \cdot \frac{(I + \iota)^\alpha}{N},
\qquad \beta(t) = R_0 \cdot \mathrm{seas}(t) \cdot (\gamma + \mu).$$

During the epidemic phase, $I \gg \iota = 2.9$, so the
per-susceptible-and-time infection rate simplifies to

$$\text{rate}(S \to E) \approx \beta \cdot s_0 \cdot I^\alpha.$$

Taking logs:

$$\log\text{rate} \approx \log\beta + \log s_0 + \alpha \log I.$$

A common simplification is to *fix β* and derive a 2-parameter
ridge in $(\log s_0, \alpha)$:

$$\log s_0 + \alpha \log I_{\text{ref}} = \text{const}
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
\boxed{\frac{d \log s_0}{d \alpha} = -\log I_{\text{ref}}}$$

with identified combination $\kappa = s_0 \cdot I_{\text{ref}}^\alpha$.
The ridge is a straight line in $(\log s_0, \alpha)$-space with
slope $-\log I_{\text{ref}}$. For He et al. London measles, $I$
during epidemics is $\sim 10^3$ to $10^4$, so the predicted slope is
**between −7 and −9**. We test this empirically below.

**But β isn't fixed in our parameterization** — it's
$\beta(t) = R_0 \cdot \mathrm{seas}(t) \cdot (\gamma + \mu)$,
where $R_0$ and $\gamma$ are *both* parameters we estimate. The
honest constant-rate condition at $I_{\text{ref}}$ is

$$\log R_0 + \log(\gamma + \mu) + \log s_0 + \alpha \log I_{\text{ref}}
\;=\; \text{const}.$$

This is a **4-parameter ridge** in $(R_0, \gamma, s_0, \alpha)$: any
joint perturbation that leaves the left-hand side invariant
produces the same rate trajectory and the same likelihood.
Fisher information along the ridge direction vanishes —
Rothenberg/Fisher non-identifiability [@rothenberg1971;
@ionides2024]. Only the ridge-aligned combination

$$\kappa \;=\; R_0 \cdot (\gamma + \mu) \cdot s_0 \cdot I_{\text{ref}}^\alpha$$

is identified.

**Numerical confirmation from the R₀ profile** (re-optimized
parameters at conditional MLEs):

- $R_0 = 20$: $\gamma = 0.120$, $\alpha = 0.83$, so
  $\beta = R_0(\gamma+\mu) \approx 2.4$
- $R_0 = 100$: $\gamma = 0.121$, $\alpha = 0.58$, so
  $\beta \approx 12.1$

β changes by a factor of 5, but α slides 0.83 → 0.58 to absorb it:
$I^{0.83} / I^{0.58} = I^{0.25}$, and with $I \sim 10^3$ during
epidemics, $I^{0.25} \approx 5.6$ — matching the β change almost
exactly. The data does not distinguish "high R₀ with weakly
super-linear FOI" from "low R₀ with more nearly linear FOI" because
they predict identical effective rates. **The 1D profiles each
trace a different cross-section of the same 4D ridge; the 2D
profiles map 2D faces of it.** There is no "fix R₀, profile s₀"
story that escapes the ridge — when you fix any one of the four,
the data slides along the other three.

The empirical-vs-theory check below uses the 2-parameter
$(s_0, \alpha)$ slice (with R₀ and γ re-optimized at each grid
point), which is the cleanest 1D test of the ridge slope. The
slope agreement with theory tests the structural prediction; the
4-parameter framing above explains why the 1D profiles on R₀
and γ are *also* flat, not just s₀.

### Empirical ridge from the s₀ profile

We compute the empirical slope by fitting α versus log s₀ over the
re-optimized profile points (excluding the descent region at very
low s₀ where the ridge approximation breaks down because $I$ is
no longer $\gg \iota$).

```{python}
#| label: fig-ridge-tradeoff
#| fig-cap: "Empirical FOI ridge. Each dot is the conditional MLE α at one s₀ grid point of the 1D profile, dot size proportional to exp(ll − max ll). The black line is the linear fit α = a + b·ln(s₀) over the ridge-active region (s₀ ≥ 0.02, where I ≫ ι). The fitted slope b corresponds to a characteristic infection level I_ref = exp(−1/b) (in natural log units), shown in the annotation."
p = _load_profile(PROF_S0).sort("s0")
s0v   = p["s0"].to_numpy()
alpha = p["alpha"].to_numpy()
ll    = p["loglik"].to_numpy()

# Ridge-active region: s0 large enough that I >> iota during epidemic.
# Use the flat part of the profile (s0 >= 0.02).
mask = s0v >= 0.02
log_s0 = np.log(s0v[mask])
a_fit  = alpha[mask]

# Linear fit α = a + b · log(s0); slope b = -1/log(I_ref)
b, a = np.polyfit(log_s0, a_fit, 1)
I_ref = np.exp(-1.0/b)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 5))
sc = ax.scatter(np.log(s0v), alpha, c=ll, cmap="viridis",
                s=80, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.6,
                label="conditional MLE α(s₀)")
xs = np.linspace(np.log(s0v[mask].min()), np.log(s0v[mask].max()), 50)
ax.plot(xs, a + b * xs, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5,
        label=f"linear fit (s₀ ≥ 0.02):\n  slope = {b:.2f} → I_ref = exp(−1/slope) = {I_ref:.0f}")
ax.scatter([np.log(TRUTH["s0"])], [TRUTH["alpha"]], marker="x",
           color="black", s=180, linewidth=3, zorder=5,
           label=f"truth (s₀={TRUTH['s0']:.3f}, α={TRUTH['alpha']:.3f})")
ax.set_xlabel("ln(s₀)"); ax.set_ylabel("α at conditional MLE")
ax.set_title("Empirical (s₀, α) ridge vs theoretical FOI prediction")
# Legend top-right (outside axes), colorbar bottom-right — stacked,
# don't clash on the right margin.
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="upper left",
          bbox_to_anchor=(1.04, 1.00))
cbar = plt.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, label="log-likelihood",
                    shrink=0.45, pad=0.04, anchor=(0.0, 0.0),
                    location="right")
fig.tight_layout()

print(f"\nFitted ridge: α = {a:.3f} + ({b:.3f}) · ln(s₀)")
print(f"Predicted slope range (I ∈ [10³, 10⁴]):  -ln(I_ref) ∈ [-9.21, -6.91]")
print(f"Observed slope: {b:.3f}  →  I_ref = {I_ref:.0f}")
print(f"This {'falls within' if -9.21 <= b <= -6.91 else 'is outside'} the predicted band.")
```

The empirical slope agrees with the FOI prediction to within the
predicted band. The fitted $I_{\text{ref}}$ lies in the
characteristic-infection range during He et al. epidemics —
confirming the derivation rather than calibrating to it.

### 2D profile — direct ridge visualization

A 2D profile over $(s_0, \alpha)$ jointly, with the other
parameters re-optimized at each grid point, traces the ridge as a
2D contour plot rather than indirectly through 1D slices. We use a
10 × 10 grid (s₀ log-spaced over [0.005, 0.45]; α linear over
[0.50, 0.99]).

```{python}
#| label: fig-profile-2d
#| fig-cap: "2D profile likelihood over (s₀, α), all other parameters re-optimized at each grid point. Color = log-likelihood. Black dashed line = theoretical ridge slope from §6. White × = truth (s₀=0.030, α=0.976). The flat-likelihood region traces the FOI ridge directly."
PROF_2D = PROFS / "profile_s0_alpha_2d.tsv"
if PROF_2D.exists():
    p2 = _load_profile(PROF_2D)
    s0_grid    = sorted(p2["s0"].unique().to_list())
    alpha_grid = sorted(p2["alpha"].unique().to_list())
    Z = np.full((len(alpha_grid), len(s0_grid)), np.nan)
    for row in p2.iter_rows(named=True):
        i = alpha_grid.index(row["alpha"])
        j = s0_grid.index(row["s0"])
        Z[i, j] = row["loglik"]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
    im = ax.pcolormesh(np.log(s0_grid), alpha_grid, Z,
                        cmap="viridis", shading="auto")
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="log-likelihood")
    ax.contour(np.log(s0_grid), alpha_grid, Z, levels=10,
               colors="white", linewidths=0.5, alpha=0.5)
    # Overlay theoretical ridge from §6
    a_intercept = TRUTH["alpha"] - b * np.log(TRUTH["s0"])
    xs2 = np.linspace(np.log(min(s0_grid)), np.log(max(s0_grid)), 50)
    ax.plot(xs2, a_intercept + b * xs2, color="black", linestyle="--",
            linewidth=1.5, label=f"theory: slope = {b:.2f}")
    ax.scatter([np.log(TRUTH["s0"])], [TRUTH["alpha"]], marker="x",
               color="white", s=180, linewidth=3, zorder=5, label="truth")
    ax.set_xlabel("ln(s₀)"); ax.set_ylabel("α")
    ax.set_title("2D profile likelihood: (s₀, α) ridge")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="center left",
              bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5))
    fig.tight_layout()
else:
    print("2D profile not yet present. Run: cd vignettes/he2010 && make profile-s0-alpha-2d")
```

The (s₀, α) plot is the cleanest visualization of the FOI ridge,
but it's only one face of a higher-dimensional ridge. The data
also fails to identify R₀ separately from (s₀, α), so we map the
remaining 2D faces.

```{python}
#| label: fig-profile-s0-r0-2d
#| fig-cap: "2D profile likelihood over (s₀, R₀), all other parameters re-optimized at each grid point. Color = log-likelihood. White × = truth (s₀=0.030, R₀=56.8). A flat ridge across the full grid means the data does not jointly identify s₀ and R₀."
PROF_2D_S0R0 = PROFS / "profile_s0_R0_2d.tsv"
if PROF_2D_S0R0.exists():
    p_s0r0 = _load_profile(PROF_2D_S0R0)
    s0g = sorted(p_s0r0["s0"].unique().to_list())
    r0g = sorted(p_s0r0["R0"].unique().to_list())
    Z2 = np.full((len(r0g), len(s0g)), np.nan)
    for row in p_s0r0.iter_rows(named=True):
        i = r0g.index(row["R0"]); j = s0g.index(row["s0"])
        Z2[i, j] = row["loglik"]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
    im = ax.pcolormesh(np.log(s0g), r0g, Z2, cmap="viridis", shading="auto")
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="log-likelihood")
    ax.contour(np.log(s0g), r0g, Z2, levels=10,
               colors="white", linewidths=0.5, alpha=0.5)
    ax.scatter([np.log(TRUTH["s0"])], [TRUTH["R0"]], marker="x",
               color="white", s=180, linewidth=3, zorder=5, label="truth")
    ax.set_xlabel("ln(s₀)"); ax.set_ylabel("R₀")
    ax.set_title("2D profile likelihood: (s₀, R₀)")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="center left",
              bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5))
    fig.tight_layout()
else:
    print("2D (s₀, R₀) profile not yet present. Run: make profile-s0-r0-2d")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-profile-alpha-r0-2d
#| fig-cap: "2D profile likelihood over (α, R₀), all other parameters re-optimized at each grid point. Color = log-likelihood. White × = truth (α=0.976, R₀=56.8)."
PROF_2D_AR0 = PROFS / "profile_alpha_R0_2d.tsv"
if PROF_2D_AR0.exists():
    p_ar0 = _load_profile(PROF_2D_AR0)
    ag  = sorted(p_ar0["alpha"].unique().to_list())
    r0g = sorted(p_ar0["R0"].unique().to_list())
    Z3 = np.full((len(r0g), len(ag)), np.nan)
    for row in p_ar0.iter_rows(named=True):
        i = r0g.index(row["R0"]); j = ag.index(row["alpha"])
        Z3[i, j] = row["loglik"]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
    im = ax.pcolormesh(ag, r0g, Z3, cmap="viridis", shading="auto")
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="log-likelihood")
    ax.contour(ag, r0g, Z3, levels=10, colors="white",
               linewidths=0.5, alpha=0.5)
    ax.scatter([TRUTH["alpha"]], [TRUTH["R0"]], marker="x",
               color="white", s=180, linewidth=3, zorder=5, label="truth")
    ax.set_xlabel("α"); ax.set_ylabel("R₀")
    ax.set_title("2D profile likelihood: (α, R₀)")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="center left",
              bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5))
    fig.tight_layout()
else:
    print("2D (α, R₀) profile not yet present. Run: make profile-alpha-r0-2d")
```
